input.routine: Wake at 6:30, snooze the alarm twice, check my phone in bed for 20 minutes before getting up, shower, coffee, commute 30 min listening to a podcast, at my desk by 9. Meetings 9-12, lunch at my desk, more meetings 1-4, try to do focused work 4-6 but usually get interrupted. Home by 7, dinner, then TV or scrolling until midnight.
input.goals: Better focus, less exhausted, want to do creative work in the evenings but never have energy
input.painPoints: The 2pm slump is brutal. I feel behind before I even start.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your day starts with two snoozes and about 20 minutes on your phone before you get out of bed. You also said you already feel behind before the day starts. That first stretch — from alarm to actually getting up — is entirely within your control and happens before meetings or other people enter the picture.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: You mentioned feeling behind before you even start. The morning phone habit is a specific, repeatable behavior that sits right at the beginning of that feeling, and it is one of the few parts of your day that does not depend on anyone else.

change_to_try.change: Before you go to sleep, place your phone somewhere you cannot reach from bed.
change_to_try.why_this_one: It is a single physical action you take the night before, so it does not require willpower in the moment. It is easy to reverse if it causes a practical problem. It targets a behavior you already identified — feeling behind before you start — and it happens before the rest of your day becomes shaped by meetings and interruptions.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: Tonight, when you finish using your phone, set it down somewhere in your home that is out of arm's reach from your bed but still within earshot if you use it as an alarm. That is the whole change. Do not adjust anything else yet.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: Reaching for your phone in the morning becomes less convenient, which removes the easiest path into the 20-minute scroll. If that causes you to get up sooner, you recover some or all of those 20 minutes at the start of your day. Whether that affects how rushed or behind you feel is something to observe — it is plausible but not guaranteed.

math.calculation: 20 minutes x 365 days = 121 hours per year currently attached to the in-bed phone habit.
math.meaning: That is the time currently attached to the behavior you are testing — not a promised saving. Whether any of it is recovered, and what you do with it, is something your actual experience will tell you.

alternatives.alternative: Stop watching TV or scrolling earlier in the evening to protect sleep time and create space for the creative work you want.
alternatives.why_not_first: The evening habit is a reasonable place to intervene, but it involves winding down a longer stretch of the day and may be harder to shift on the first try. The morning phone change is a single action taken the night before and does not compete with anything else in the moment.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You get out of bed closer to when the alarm first goes off.
You recover some of the 20 minutes and arrive at your morning routine feeling less rushed.
The sense of already being behind is less pronounced on mornings when you try this.
signs_to_rethink_it: You simply retrieve the phone and scroll from wherever it is — the habit moves but does not change.
The placement creates a practical problem, such as not hearing your alarm.
You try it for several mornings and nothing about how you feel at the start of the day is different.

input.routine: Wake 7am, gym 7:30-8:30, work from home 9-6 (freelance), lunch whenever, afternoon is usually most productive, evenings free but I end up working anyway. Bed around 1am. Sleep is bad.
input.goals: Better sleep, stop working evenings, make progress on a side project
input.painPoints: I have freedom but feel less productive than when I had an office job.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your workday is nominally 9-6, but you also work most evenings and go to bed around 1am. You said afternoons are your most productive stretch, which means your strongest working hours are already inside the official window — yet the day keeps extending anyway.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: All three things you want to improve — sleep, stopping evening work, and making time for a side project — run into the same obstacle: there is no defined point where work ends. Without a clear stop, the evening stays available to work, which pushes bed later and leaves no protected time for anything else.

change_to_try.change: Pick one specific time as a daily work stop — say, 6pm, since that is already the end of your stated workday — and treat it as a hard close: log off, close work tabs or apps, and do not reopen them until the next morning.
change_to_try.why_this_one: You already have a nominal end time of 6pm, so this is not inventing a new structure — it is making the one you described actually function as a boundary. It is small, reversible, and requires no new tools or schedule changes. It also sits at the junction of all three goals you mentioned: stopping evening work, creating a window where the side project could happen, and giving sleep a better chance by separating wind-down time from work.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: At 6pm, close whatever you are working on — even if it feels unfinished — and physically close or quit the work apps or browser tabs. Treat the open task as something for tomorrow morning, not tonight. If something genuinely urgent comes up, handle it as an exception rather than a habit.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: The direct effect is simple: work stops at 6pm instead of continuing into the evening. That creates a block of unscheduled time that is not currently available. Whether you use that block for the side project, winding down, or something else is up to you — but the time exists in a way it currently does not. If work stops earlier and you use the evening differently, going to bed closer to a reasonable hour becomes more plausible, though whether that improves your sleep is something to observe rather than assume.

alternatives.alternative: Set a fixed bedtime and work backward from there.
alternatives.why_not_first: A fixed bedtime is a reasonable place to intervene, but it does not change what happens in the evening — you could still work until 12:45 and technically hit a 1am bedtime. Stopping work at 6pm changes the shape of the evening first, which gives a bedtime target something to work with.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You actually stop working at or near 6pm most evenings without a specific urgent reason to continue.
You have unscheduled evening time and use some of it for the side project.
You get into bed noticeably earlier than 1am at least some nights.
The work that did not get finished at 6pm turns out to be handleable the next morning.
signs_to_rethink_it: You stop at 6pm but then feel too unsettled to do anything else, and the side project still does not happen.
Freelance deadlines or client expectations make a 6pm stop genuinely impractical on most days.
You close work but immediately fill the time with something that still keeps you up until 1am.
The constraint creates stress that outweighs any benefit — in which case a later but still fixed stop time might fit better.
